title: Simulating the non-Hermitian dynamics of financial option pricing with quantum computers
abstract_summary: This paper generalises quantum imaginary time evolution to simulate arbitrary non-Hermitian dynamics (QNUTE), enabling the simulation of linear PDEs equivalent to the Schrödinger equation, notably the Black–Scholes equation for option pricing. The authors present a Trotter-based method that approximates non-unitary evolution with sequences of local unitary approximations, introduce a norm-correction strategy using linear boundary conditions, and demonstrate numerical simulations that price various European options matching analytical solutions while discussing measurement and scalability considerations.
methodology_description: The authors develop and numerically implement a generalisation of quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) called Quantum Non-Unitary Time Evolution (QNUTE) to simulate arbitrary non-Hermitian dynamics and thereby solve linear PDEs such as the Black–Scholes equation. They discretise the asset-price domain [x0,xN] into 2^n grid points (spacing h = (xN-x0)/(2^n - 1)) and store normalised samples of the option price as amplitudes of an n-qubit state. The continuum Black–Scholes operator is represented by a finite-difference matrix (central differences for interior points; forward/backward first-order differences at boundaries when imposing linear boundary conditions) and then decomposed into Pauli-operator strings to produce a Hamiltonian decomposition H = sum_m i h_m. Non-unitary evolution e^{-i H Δt} is approximated by first-order Trotter products over terms e^{h_m Δt}; the normalised action of each local non-unitary factor e^{h_m Δt} on the current state |ψ⟩ is approximated by a unitary e^{-i A Δt} where A = sum_I a_I σ_I is Hermitian. The coefficients a_I are obtained at each Trotter step by solving a linear system (S + S^T) a = b constructed from expectation-value measurements on |ψ⟩, where S_{I,J}=⟨ψ|σ_I^† σ_J|ψ⟩, c = sqrt(1 + 2 Δt Re⟨ψ|h_m|ψ⟩) and b_I = -2 c Im⟨ψ|σ_I^† h_m|ψ⟩, yielding an O(I^2) measurement cost per term and O(I) circuit depth per local unitary. They consider both exact (unitaries acting on all correlated qubits) and inexact implementations where the Hermitian approximation A is restricted to act on D adjacent qubits (D < correlation length), analyse fidelity degradation for inexact domains, and incorporate a norm-correction/rescaling strategy by encoding linear boundary ODE behaviour (a(τ)=a(0), b(τ)=b(0) e^{-r τ}) into the Hamiltonian and rescaling normalised solutions accordingly. Complexity statements and resource scalings (measurements O(N_T M I^2), Trotter step count N_T = T/Δt, circuit depths, and choice of σ_I operator sets) are provided, and the method is demonstrated in numerical simulations of various European payoffs (calls, puts, spreads, straddles, strangles) over an asset domain [0,150] with example parameters (T, N_T, r, σ) reported in their experiments.
algorithms_used: Simulated QITE (simulated Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution)
key_findings: [speculative] The authors generalise quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to simulate arbitrary non-Hermitian dynamics (QNUTE), removing the anti-Hermitian restriction.

[speculative] QNUTE approximates non-unitary time evolution via first-order Trotterisation of a decomposition ˆH = ∑ iˆhm and approximates each local non-unitary e^{ˆhm∆t} by a unitary e^{-iˆA∆t} found by solving a linear system based on measurements.

[speculative] Theoretical resource scaling: each Trotter step requires O(I^2) measurements to construct an I×I linear system, circuits of depth O(I), and full simulation costs O(N_T M I^2) measurements.

[speculative] The number of Hermitian operator terms I needed to express local approximations grows exponentially with the local domain size D (I = O(2^D)) when expressed in Pauli strings, causing an exponential overhead.

[supported] The authors numerically implemented QNUTE (classical simulation of the algorithm) to price various European options (call, put, bull/bear spread, straddle, strangle) modelled by the Black–Scholes PDE and obtained close agreement with analytical solutions under chosen discretisation and boundary conditions.

[supported] Numerical results show that when the unitary approximations act on all qubits (exact/untruncated domain) the QNUTE simulations match analytical Black–Scholes solutions for the tested cases (examples shown for n up to 6 qubits, NT=500, T=3 years).

[supported] Inexact QNUTE implementations that restrict unitaries to a smaller domain size D < n yield low average fidelities for the Black–Scholes Hamiltonian when correlation length is large; fidelity degrades with increasing number of qubits if D is held small.

[supported] The authors introduce and apply a norm-correction (rescaling) strategy based on imposing linear boundary conditions for option prices at domain boundaries (u(x,τ) ≈ a(τ)x + b(τ)) and using the resulting boundary ODE to rescale normalised states during evolution.

[speculative] The paper asserts QNUTE can be used to approximate solutions to arbitrary linear PDEs (with solutions stored in qubit amplitudes) and that relevant solution information can be extracted with a polynomial number of distinct measurements in the number of qubits.

[speculative] The authors claim that time-dependent volatility and interest rates can be encoded in the Hamiltonian without extra construction cost, though stochastic modelling may require smaller time steps.

[speculative] They propose that adopting alternative measurement/decomposition schemes (e.g., measuring finite-difference operators per Liu et al.) could reduce the exponential number of Hamiltonian terms and improve scalability.

[speculative] Compared to prior approaches, they claim QNUTE directly simulates the original (non-Hermitian) Black–Scholes operator without relying on variable-change to anti-Hermitian form (varQITE) nor on post-selection approaches.
results_summary: The authors develop QNUTE, a theoretical extension of QITE to arbitrary non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and detail how to approximate each local non-unitary Trotter factor by a unitary via a measurement-driven linear solve. They implement classical numerical simulations of the method to price several European option payoffs under the Black–Scholes PDE, using discretisation and linear boundary conditions with norm rescaling, and report close agreement with analytical solutions when unitary approximations cover the full domain. They observe large fidelity loss for inexact (small-domain) unitaries due to strong correlations in the discretised Hamiltonian, and identify an exponential overhead in Pauli-term decomposition as a key scalability challenge while suggesting potential mitigations.
performance_claims: Simulation parameters used: domain x ∈ [0,150], maturity T = 3 years, N_T = 500 time steps, risk-free r = 0.04, volatility σ = 0.2.
Resource scaling claim: full simulation requires O(N_T M I^2) measurements; each Trotter step needs O(I^2) measurements and circuit depth O(I).
Operator count scaling: I = O(2^D) when using Pauli-string decomposition on a domain of D adjacent qubits.

Fidelity examples (mean ± std) from Table 1: for Call and Put with n=2, D=2 mean fidelity µ_F = 1.000 (σ_F ≈ 2.7×10^-5 and 4.5×10^-5 respectively); for n=3, D=2 µ_F ≈ 0.994 (σ_F ≈ 4.77×10^-3) for Call and µ_F ≈ 0.982 (σ_F ≈ 1.20×10^-2) for Put.
Representative low-fidelity inexact examples: for n=5, D=2 the Call mean fidelity µ_F ≈ 0.158 (σ_F ≈ 0.211) and Put µ_F ≈ 0.749 (σ_F ≈ 0.0679), indicating large degradation when D < n.
Exact-domain simulations (unitaries acting on all qubits) achieved near-unity fidelities for tested n up to 6 (many entries show µ_F ≈ 1.000 with very small σ_F).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper proposes a quantum-algorithmic framework (QNUTE) and shows classical numerical simulations of its behaviour, but does not demonstrate a runtime or resource advantage on quantum hardware nor prove asymptotic quantum speedup. Scalability challenges (exponential Pauli decomposition, measurement overhead) are acknowledged and mitigations are proposed, leaving any practical quantum advantage unproven and speculative.
limitations: The Hamiltonian decomposition into Pauli strings scales exponentially with the number of qubits (number of distinct Pauli terms ∼ O(2^D)), making the approach non-scalable in its current form for large systems (author-stated).

QNUTE requires unitary approximations with support size D that should ideally cover the correlation length C; when using inexact QNUTE with domain size D < C, fidelities drop substantially (author-stated / demonstrated).
The measurement complexity is high: each Trotter step requires O(I^2) measurements and the full simulation O(NT M I^2), which can be prohibitive (author-stated).

Norm / scale-factor errors compound across many Trotter steps and require periodic correction; the correction strategy used relies on boundary behaviour and is nontrivial because the discretised Black–Scholes Hamiltonian is non-normal (author-stated).

The norm correction approach depends on enforcing linear boundary conditions and on having suitable boundary behaviour; if those assumptions fail, the rescaling strategy is not directly applicable (author-stated / implied).
Current numerical demonstrations use unitaries acting on all qubits (i.e., full support), which may be impractical on NISQ devices (author-stated implication from experiments).
Simulations assume constant volatility (σ) and constant risk-free rate (r); stochastic/time-dependent parameters would likely require smaller time steps and increase cost (author-stated).

[inferred] Extracting pointwise, non-normalised solution values presumes the solution is real and non-negative so that square roots of measurement probabilities yield values; this may limit applicability to PDEs with sign-changing or complex solutions.

[inferred] The approach currently relies on classical computations for solving the linear systems (S + S^T) a = b each step and on measuring many expectation values, implying significant classical overhead and potential bottlenecks.

[inferred] The requirement to choose a set of basis operators {σ_I} (and its support size D) introduces a trade-off between expressivity and resource cost; there is no prescriptive method given to pick them optimally.
[inferred] Numerical results are simulation-based; the method’s robustness to realistic hardware noise and gate errors on current quantum devices is not demonstrated.
[inferred] The Trotter approximation and first-order Trotter steps used introduce discretisation errors in time; error scaling and mitigation strategies are not analysed in depth.
open_questions: How can the exponential number of Pauli terms in the Hamiltonian decomposition be reduced to make QNUTE scalable for larger qubit counts?
What is the effect on accuracy and resource requirements when integrating recent QITE improvements (Fast QITE, time-dependent drifted QITE, nonlocal approximation) into the QNUTE framework?

Can the expectation-measurement scheme proposed by Liu et al. (linear overhead) be adapted to QNUTE to achieve an exponential reduction in Hamiltonian terms, and how would that affect total complexity?
How should one choose the operator basis {σ_I} and the support domain size D optimally given a target Hamiltonian with correlation length C?
How can norm correction be performed reliably for non-normal, non-Hermitian discretised Hamiltonians when boundary conditions are non-linear or unknown?
How does QNUTE perform on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, i.e., what is its noise tolerance and required error rates for useful accuracy?
What are the precise measurement and gate-count trade-offs for realistic option-pricing instances (larger grids, multiple assets, path-dependent payoffs) when using QNUTE?
How to extend QNUTE to PDEs whose solutions are sign-changing or complex-valued, where the simple probability-sqrt readout is not applicable?
How to incorporate stochastic volatility or stochastic interest rate models into QNUTE efficiently (beyond the note that they increase time-step requirements)?

How does QNUTE compare—both in resources and accuracy—to other quantum approaches for Black–Scholes (e.g., variational QITE methods, Hamiltonian simulation with post-selection) in practical problem sizes?
What are the stability and convergence guarantees (error bounds) for QNUTE when applied to general linear PDEs beyond the examples shown?
Can one devise more efficient classical-quantum hybrid strategies for solving the per-step linear systems (S + S^T) a = b to reduce classical overhead?

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — QNUTE generalises QITE to approximate non-Hermitian (Black–Scholes) dynamics by Trotterising local non-unitary factors and approximating each via a measurement-driven classical linear solve to produce local unitaries.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — The authors demonstrate classical numerical simulations (up to n=6 qubits, NT=500) that reproduce analytical European option prices, and analyse fidelity degradation when restricting local unitaries to smaller domains (D < correlation length).

#idea:quantum-advantage — The paper claims that option-PDE solutions can be stored in qubit amplitudes and that relevant information can be extracted with polynomially many distinct measurements, and suggests direct simulation of the non-Hermitian Black–Scholes operator avoids some prior workarounds.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Norm-correction/rescaling using linear boundary ODEs is introduced as a classical post-processing step to correct normalization when encoding option boundary behaviour into the Hamiltonian.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Detailed resource accounting is provided (measurements O(N_T M I^2), circuit depth O(I) per local unitary) and numerical experiments illustrate practical measurement and fidelity trade-offs.
contradictions: The paper asserts that relevant solution information can be extracted with a polynomial number of measurements, but also shows that the number of Pauli terms I for local domains grows as I = O(2^D) and that measurement cost per Trotter step is O(I^2), implying an exponential overhead that undermines the polynomial-extraction claim (internal scalability contradiction).

The authors demonstrate accurate small-scale (n≤6) simulator results and propose relevance to practical quantum computing, yet they also report severe fidelity degradation for inexact (truncated) implementations and highlight large measurement/qubit requirements — so no empirical quantum advantage over classical methods is demonstrated, contradicting any implicit claims of near-term superiority.
